Epiphenomenalism is the idea that the universe works by means of accident or small, specific arrangements rather than through a single grand explanation. In the phrase “from many things,” something is inferred from many things to produce a particular outcome—a natural discovery, a design, or an ad hoc explanation. Thus, “whirling dervishes” are personified as accidental objects controlling simple arrangements: a stray person, a set of nearby objects, or a repeating event. Epiphenomenalism rejects the tautology of necessity and demands that even the world’s simplest patterns have a history or cause.

It is closely connected to Lovelock’s ecological writing, in which natural systems are reduced to coordinated structures. Lovelock constructs organisms as wheels, wheels that can be adapted rapidly, creating a provisional stock of non-necessary explanations that may reveal surprising designs. Although “epiphenomenalism” can carry Lovelock’s meaning literally, later phrases such as “good design, simple living” show that the emphasized simplicity is not its whole law. In Lovelock’s account, natural “design” is merely one interpretation of accidental causation; other explanations may draw from less specific local arrangements, ecology, or the universe’s richness.
